stops.name: Longwood, arrival on Saint Helena
stops.campa: After a second abdication in Paris and two months of British custody aboard the Bellerophon and the Northumberland, Napoleon lands on Saint Helena, a volcanic speck in the South Atlantic chosen for its total isolation, and is housed at Longwood, a damp, rat-infested former cattle farm two thousand feet above the sea. Governor Hudson Lowe restricts his movements, opens his mail, and insists on addressing him only as 'General Bonaparte'; Napoleon, in return, refuses most invitations from a jailer he will not dignify with courtesy. He plants a garden, dictates history to whoever will write it down, and settles, at forty-six, the master of Europe eleven months before, into the last exile.
stops.quote: I would rather be a poor peasant in a country cottage than a king kept like me.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon at Longwood, recorded conversation (Las Cases, Mémorial de Sainte-Hélène)

stops.name: Longwood, Las Cases and the Memorial
stops.campa: In the small damp rooms of Longwood the comte de Las Cases, chamberlain and interpreter, begins the daily discipline that will become the Mémorial de Sainte-Hélène: hours of dictation on the campaigns, the Consulate, the Code, and the theory of war, taken down each evening and copied fair by his own son. Napoleon shapes, sentence by sentence, the account of himself that will outlive the Bourbon restoration and the Bourbon histories written against him: the Revolution's heir, not its gravedigger; the liberator of peoples, not their conqueror. Las Cases is deported by Lowe within the year for smuggling letters, but the notebooks travel with him, and the legend they contain reaches Paris years before the body does.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon to Las Cases, aboard the Bellerophon, August 1815, on the purpose of exile

stops.name: Longwood, the death of the Emperor
stops.campa: After months of wasting illness, stomach pain, vomiting, a decline his doctors misread almost to the end, Napoleon dictates a will dividing his modest fortune among his family and old soldiers, asks that his ashes rest on the Seine among the French people he loved, and dies at Longwood in the late afternoon, a violent storm breaking over the island at the hour of his death. Witnesses who lean close to catch his last words hear only fragments: France, the army, head of the army, and, some swear, Joséphine's name at the very end. He is buried, at Lowe's insistence, under an unmarked stone in the Sane Valley.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon's last words, variously recorded by attendants at Longwood, 5 May 1821

stops.name: Les Invalides, the retour des cendres
stops.campa: Nineteen years after Longwood, on the initiative of minister Thiers, eager to borrow the dead Emperor's glory for a shaky monarchy, the frigate Belle Poule, commanded by the Prince de Joinville, carries the exhumed and startlingly well-preserved body home across the winter Atlantic. Through a snowstorm the gilded funeral chariot, drawn under the Arc de Triomphe and down the Champs-Élysées, brings the coffin to the Dôme des Invalides before six hundred thousand Parisians massed in the cold: the eagle's flight completed at last, the towers of Notre-Dame outdone by the dome under which he will lie, twenty years dead and, the crowd senses, not at all finished with France.
stops.quote: I desire that my ashes may repose on the banks of the Seine, among the French people whom I have loved so well.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon's will, Longwood, 1821, the wish fulfilled by the retour des cendres, 1840
